claims.text: Berkeley Earth reports that since late August 2025 GSOD, GHCN-Daily and GHCN-Monthly have been broken or degraded, cutting its station intake from ~20,000 a month to ~15,000 in late 2025; it gives no cause. UCS (May 2026) repeats this as 6,000 of 20,000 stations.

evidence.passage: Since late August 2025, core NOAA climate archives, including the Global Summary of the Day, Global Historical Climatology Network – Daily, and Global Historical Climatology Network – Monthly (GHCN-M), have been broken or incomplete. … In the case of GHCN-M, which is NOAA’s flagship climate monitoring platform, the defects are strongly clustered with NOAA failing to report nearly all observations from China, Kazakhstan, the Philippines, Spain, and certain other areas. … As a result, the maps have unusual gaps in Africa and the land-average uncertainty has temporarily spiked to a ~50 year high.
evidence.location: section 'Continuing NOAA Data Problems', text lines 34-42

evidence.passage: Since late August 2025, core NOAA climate archives, including the Global Summary of the Day, Global Historical Climatology Network – Daily, and Global Historical Climatology Network – Monthly (GHCN-M), have been either broken or in a degraded state. … While we ordinarily expect to have weather data from ~20,000 weather stations per month in the modern period, the disruption to NOAA services has cut that number to ~15,000 during late 2025. Due to additional delays in reporting, the February data set is reduced even further to ~6,000 stations. … NOAA’s pending launch of the Synoptic Summary of the Day (a replacement for the Global Summary of the Day) should also help, though the expected timeline for that launch is unknown.
evidence.location: section 'Continuing NOAA Data Problems', text lines 51-55

evidence.passage: Since late August 2025, core NOAA climate archives, including the Global Summary of the Day, Global Historical Climatology Network – Daily, and Global Historical Climatology Network – Monthly (GHCN-M), have been either broken or in a degraded state. … While we ordinarily expect to have weather data from ~20,000 weather stations per month in the modern period, the disruption to NOAA services has cut that number to ~15,000 during late 2025. Due to additional delays in reporting, the March data set is reduced even further to ~6,700 stations. … We wish to note that this situation has been slowly improving with some of the missing stations having been restored in recent months. NOAA’s launch of the Synoptic Summary of the Day (a replacement for the Global Summary of the Day) should also help. … We expect the problems with NOAA data aggregation will ultimately be temporary, as the underlying weather stations still exist, and it is simply a matter of getting suitable access.
evidence.location: section 'Continuing NOAA Data Problems', lines 45-55 of text

One of NOAA’s core climate archives, the Global Historical Climatological Network, is still facing severe disruptions, with only about 6,000 of its 20,000 observational stations reporting valuable weather and climate information.
